items.content_html:
Cable tray systems are often described simply as pathways for electrical cables, but in commercial, industrial, healthcare, and infrastructure construction, a complete cable tray installation is an engineered support and routing assembly. The tray must accommodate the required cable population while its supports, connections, structural attachments, and—where applicable—seismic restraints transfer loads safely into the building structure.

A technically sound cable tray design therefore involves much more than selecting a tray width. Engineers and contractors must consider cable weight, fill, tray geometry, support span, deflection, material, environmental exposure, connection capacity, structural attachment points, installation tolerances, and coordination with other MEP systems. In seismic regions, the design also needs to address earthquake-induced movement and the resulting force path through the tray, support assembly, anchorage, and supporting structure.

The distinction between ordinary cable tray support and seismic restraint is particularly important. Gravity supports carry the tray and its contents under normal conditions, while seismic bracing is intended to control applicable earthquake-induced movement. Both can be part of the same installation, but they perform different engineering functions.

These considerations become more demanding in hospitals, data centers, manufacturing plants, high-rise buildings, and critical infrastructure, where electrical distribution systems may carry substantial cable loads and where access, reliability, coordination, and documentation are important project requirements.

For projects requiring integrated engineering and fabrication, The Sigma Source brings together seismic bracing, structural engineering, seismic calculations, BIM 3D CAD modeling, and custom metal fabrication. This allows cable tray support to be considered as part of the larger structural and MEP system rather than as an isolated electrical component.

What Are Cable Tray Systems and How Are They Used in U.S. Construction?

A cable tray systems provides a continuous, accessible route for electrical and communications cabling while maintaining the physical support required by the installation. The system can include the tray, fittings, splice plates, couplers, covers, brackets, hangers, trapeze supports, strut channels, structural attachments, and seismic restraints.

Different tray configurations serve different applications. Ladder cable trays provide open rungs and ventilation and are widely used for power and industrial cable routing. Solid-bottom and perforated trays provide different levels of cable support and protection. Wire-mesh trays are frequently useful for smaller communication, data, and control cables where flexibility and accessibility are important. Channel trays can serve smaller cable groups or specific routing conditions.

Cable tray systems may carry power cables, control wiring, communication cables, fiber-optic systems, instrumentation, fire alarm wiring, and building automation cabling. In industrial facilities, trays can form an important part of process electrical distribution. In commercial buildings and high-rise facilities, they may support electrical distribution and low-voltage systems across mechanical and electrical rooms.

Healthcare facilities introduce additional coordination requirements because electrical infrastructure can serve critical systems and must coexist with dense mechanical, plumbing, architectural, and structural layouts. Data centers similarly require careful cable routing because high-density communication and power distribution can create substantial tray loading and complex spatial requirements.

The complete system should therefore be viewed as a structural chain:

Cable → Cable Tray → Support/Hanger → Strut or Bracket → Structural Attachment → Building Structure

Where seismic restraint is required, that chain expands to include the seismic brace or restraint assembly and its associated connections. This broader perspective provides the foundation for cable tray engineering and helps prevent the common mistake of treating the tray itself as the only engineered component.

How Do Engineers Select the Right Cable Tray Configuration?

Cable tray selection begins with the cables that the system must carry. Engineers need to understand the quantity, type, size, weight, routing, separation requirements, and anticipated future capacity before selecting tray dimensions and configuration.

Tray width and depth affect both cable capacity and physical coordination. A tray that is technically large enough for the initial cable population may not be appropriate if future expansion, cable separation, access, or project specifications require additional capacity. Conversely, oversizing a tray can increase weight and support requirements without providing meaningful project benefits.

Tray geometry also changes at transitions. Elbows, tees, crosses, reducers, and vertical bends introduce localized conditions that need to remain compatible with the support layout. Long horizontal runs may behave differently from vertical sections or heavily loaded transition areas. Supports should not simply be placed according to a generic pattern without considering the actual routing geometry.

Environmental conditions are another important factor. Indoor commercial applications may allow conventional coated steel or aluminum, while outdoor, industrial, coastal, or corrosive environments may require more deliberate material and finish selection. Stainless steel can be appropriate where corrosion resistance is particularly important, while galvanized or coated steel can provide suitable protection for many other environments.

The tray material also interacts with its support system. Aluminum cable trays, steel trays, stainless assemblies, structural steel brackets, galvanized components, and stainless hardware each have different physical and environmental characteristics. Dissimilar-metal interfaces should be considered where corrosion or galvanic interaction could become an issue.

Finally, cable tray selection should be coordinated with available structural attachment points and surrounding MEP systems. A tray that fits electrically may not fit physically once HVAC ducts, piping, fire protection, lighting, structural members, and maintenance clearances are included. Early engineering coordination can therefore prevent a tray selection from creating downstream support and installation problems.

How Is Cable Tray Load Capacity and Support Spacing Determined?

Cable tray support design starts with loading. The cable population contributes dead load, while the tray, fittings, covers, support hardware, and other permanent components also contribute to the supported weight. Project conditions may additionally require consideration of concentrated loads, installation conditions, impact, or other applicable loading criteria.

Support spacing is not a universal number. It depends on tray type, material, dimensions, span, loading, manufacturer performance data, allowable deflection, support configuration, and project requirements. A longer support span can increase bending demand and deflection, while shorter spans can increase the number of structural attachments and installation points.

For this reason, engineers need to evaluate the tray and support assembly as a system. Consider a heavily loaded ladder tray supported by threaded rods and a strut trapeze. The tray may have adequate capacity, but the complete assembly still depends on the capacity of the cross member, rods, fittings, brackets, anchors, and supporting structure. The weakest connection can govern the system.

Localized loading also deserves attention. A cable tray may have a generally distributed cable load but encounter a concentrated load during installation or maintenance. Support geometry should be reviewed accordingly where project criteria require it.

Deflection can be important even when ultimate strength is adequate. Excessive movement can affect cable routing, connections, clearances, fittings, or the appearance and serviceability of the installation. Engineers therefore need to consider both strength and serviceability.

Manufacturer load tables are valuable design inputs, but they should be applied within their stated assumptions. Tray configuration, support span, loading pattern, splice conditions, and installation orientation can affect the applicability of published values.

The engineering chain can be expressed as:

Cable Weight → Tray Capacity → Support Span → Support Capacity → Connection Capacity → Structural Capacity

This approach prevents a common design error: checking the tray while overlooking the support and structural attachment that actually transfers its load.

What Types of Cable Tray Support Systems Are Used?

Cable tray support systems vary according to tray geometry, building structure, available space, loading, and installation requirements. One of the most common configurations for horizontal tray runs is the trapeze support, which can use threaded rods and a strut channel or fabricated cross member beneath the tray.

Strut channel systems are particularly useful because they provide adjustable framing for brackets, trapezes, rails, and support assemblies. Single or double strut configurations can be selected according to the required geometry and loading. Fittings allow the support structure to be assembled around existing conditions, while custom strut channels can address dimensions or interfaces that standard components cannot accommodate efficiently.

Cable tray brackets provide another solution where the tray can be supported from a wall, column, structural member, or other suitable attachment point. Hangers and support rails may be used for specific layouts or smaller tray configurations. Larger or heavily loaded systems can require fabricated support frames that distribute loads across multiple structural attachment points.

The selection of a support system should consider more than whether the tray can physically sit on it. The support needs adequate stiffness and capacity, and its attachment to the building must be appropriate for the imposed loads.

For example, a cable tray may be positioned below a structural beam where a trapeze arrangement is practical. Another installation may have limited overhead space, requiring a wall-mounted bracket. A retrofit project may have an existing concrete slab with restricted anchor locations, requiring a custom attachment plate or alternate support geometry.

In seismic applications, ordinary supports may also need to work with seismic restraint assemblies. The support should not interfere with brace geometry, and the complete arrangement should provide a clear load path.

The Sigma Source can integrate strut channel systems, custom support frames, structural attachment plates, seismic restraint assemblies, and custom fabricated steel components when project conditions require a coordinated solution rather than a standard support arrangement.

How Is Cable Tray Anchorage Connected to the Building Structure?

Cable tray anchorage establishes the interface between the support system and the building structure. This interface is critical because the capacity of a tray or bracket does not automatically establish the capacity of the complete installation.

The load path can be represented as:

Cable Load → Tray → Support → Connection → Anchor → Structural Member

Every link in that chain needs to be compatible with the applicable design loads.

For concrete attachments, engineers may evaluate mechanical or adhesive anchors, attachment plates, edge distances, embedment conditions, concrete strength, reinforcement conflicts, and the capacity of the supporting substrate. The specific anchor type and installation method need to be appropriate for the actual project conditions.

Steel-to-steel connections can involve beam clamps, bolted brackets, welded assemblies, attachment plates, gusset plates, or other engineered connections. The structural member itself must be capable of receiving the transferred load without creating an unacceptable local condition.

Existing buildings introduce additional uncertainty. Drawings may not completely represent current structural conditions, and retrofit work can encounter concealed reinforcement, existing anchors, damaged concrete, inaccessible steel, or other field conditions. Field verification can therefore be an important part of the engineering process.

Seismic applications make the load path even more important. An earthquake restraint may develop forces that are transferred through a brace into a connection and then into the structural member. Designing only the brace without evaluating its attachment can leave a significant portion of the load path unresolved.

Coordination between structural and MEP disciplines is particularly valuable here. The electrical team establishes the tray routing and system requirements, while structural engineering evaluates how the support and restraint loads interact with the building.

For complex installations, BIM and CAD models can help identify available structural attachment points before fabrication. This makes it possible to develop support assemblies around actual building geometry rather than discovering conflicts after components have been manufactured.

What Is Cable Tray Seismic Bracing and When Is It Required?

Cable tray seismic bracing is designed to control earthquake-induced movement of a cable tray system and transfer applicable seismic forces through a defined structural load path. It is fundamentally different from ordinary gravity support.

A conventional support holds the tray under its normal vertical loading. During an earthquake, however, the tray can experience lateral movement and forces resulting from the motion of the building. Depending on the applicable project requirements, additional restraints may be necessary to control movement in one or more directions.

The engineering process begins with project-specific seismic criteria. Relevant considerations can include the adopted building code, ASCE 7 requirements, Seismic Design Category, Risk Category, component characteristics, project specifications, and requirements established by the Engineer of Record.

ASCE 7 Chapter 13 can be relevant to nonstructural component seismic design, but requirements should not be applied as a generic formula independent of the actual project. The adopted code edition, jurisdiction, component classification, supporting structure, and project-specific criteria all matter.

Seismic cable tray support can include rigid braces, strut-based assemblies, cable bracing, transverse restraints, longitudinal restraints, or other engineered configurations. The appropriate arrangement depends on the tray layout and design requirements.

The seismic load path should be clear:

Cable Tray → Seismic Restraint → Brace Connection → Anchorage → Structural Member

This is especially important in high-seismic regions and critical facilities. Healthcare projects under HCAI jurisdiction may involve specific seismic and documentation requirements that need to be coordinated with the overall project design.

Seismic restraint also needs to coexist with normal cable tray support. Adding a brace to an otherwise incomplete support system does not automatically create a compliant seismic assembly. The tray, supports, braces, connections, and structural attachments must work together.

The Sigma Source's work in seismic bracing and structural engineering provides a natural framework for addressing cable tray systems where electrical routing must be integrated with structural seismic restraint.

How Do Transverse and Longitudinal Cable Tray Braces Work?

Cable tray seismic restraints are commonly discussed in terms of the direction of movement they are intended to control. Transverse restraint addresses movement generally perpendicular to the tray's longitudinal direction, while longitudinal restraint addresses movement along the primary direction of the tray.

A horizontal cable tray running through a large mechanical or electrical room may therefore require restraint in multiple directions depending on the applicable engineering criteria. Four-way or two-way restraint configurations can be developed according to the geometry and required force directions.

Brace configuration must be coordinated with the tray support system. A brace attached to a trapeze assembly transfers load through that assembly, which means the trapeze, threaded rods, strut, fittings, and structural attachments all become part of the relevant load path.

The structural connection is equally important. A brace may have substantial theoretical capacity, but its usefulness depends on whether its attachment to concrete or structural steel can safely transfer the required force. Anchor capacity, connection geometry, edge conditions, and structural member capacity may therefore govern the design.

Tray joints and building movement also require attention. Cable tray systems may pass through areas containing expansion joints or other movement interfaces. A seismic restraint strategy should not unintentionally lock together building portions that are designed to move independently.

Flexible electrical connections may be necessary where electrical systems cross movement joints or connect to equipment subject to relative movement. Seismic expansion joints can also become relevant in specific building configurations.

For contractors, the practical objective is a coordinated installation in which support locations, brace locations, structural attachments, and tray fittings are clearly defined. For engineers, the objective is a defensible load path from the supported electrical system into the structure.

BIM coordination can make this process considerably more effective by showing the tray, support assembly, structural member, and brace in the same three-dimensional environment.

How Should Cable Tray Systems Be Coordinated With MEP and Building Systems?

Cable trays rarely occupy an isolated space. In a typical commercial or industrial building, they may run alongside HVAC ductwork, mechanical piping, plumbing, fire protection, conduit, lighting, equipment, and structural framing. As tray sizes and cable quantities increase, support coordination becomes a major part of installation planning.

Structural coordination begins with available attachment points. A tray may follow an electrically logical route but encounter beams, joists, slabs, walls, or columns that prevent the planned support arrangement. Moving the tray later may create conflicts with another trade, making early coordination more efficient than field modification.

Mechanical coordination is equally important. Large ducts and pipes can occupy the same ceiling zones required by cable tray supports. A trapeze support that works in an isolated drawing may be impossible to install after adjacent systems are installed.

BIM 3D CAD provides a useful coordination environment for these conditions. Tray routing can be modeled alongside structural framing and MEP systems, allowing potential clashes to be identified before fabrication or installation. Support frames and brackets can then be developed around the actual available space.

Maintenance access should also be considered. Cable trays need sufficient accessibility for cable installation, inspection, replacement, and future modifications. Crowding a tray against another system may solve an immediate routing problem while creating a long-term maintenance problem.

Building movement adds another layer. Thermal movement, seismic separation, and expansion joints may require flexible interfaces or deliberate system discontinuities. Cable tray routing should therefore account for the building's movement strategy rather than treating the tray as a completely rigid continuous line.

An integrated workflow can be summarized as:

Electrical Layout → Structural Coordination → MEP Coordination → Support Design → Seismic Review → BIM/CAD → Fabrication → Installation

This approach is particularly valuable in hospitals, data centers, industrial plants, and other facilities where electrical reliability and coordination are closely tied to the overall building infrastructure.

What Materials Are Used for Cable Tray and Support Systems?

Material selection for cable tray systems should consider loading, structural requirements, corrosion exposure, environmental conditions, fabrication methods, and project specifications. There is no single material that is appropriate for every installation.

Steel cable trays and structural steel supports are common where strength, stiffness, and robust support construction are important. Carbon steel can be fabricated into brackets, frames, attachment plates, and other components, while galvanized or coated steel can provide corrosion protection where the operating environment permits.

Aluminum cable trays can reduce component weight and may be advantageous in applications where corrosion resistance and lower mass are desirable. However, the tray material still needs to be evaluated together with its supports and connections.

Stainless steel can be appropriate in environments where corrosion resistance is a major consideration. Stainless steel hardware may also be selected for specific environmental or compatibility requirements.

Protective finishes such as galvanizing and powder coating can extend service life when appropriately matched to the environment and operating conditions. The suitability of a coating depends on exposure, temperature, surface preparation, mechanical damage, and project specifications.

Material compatibility should extend to fasteners and connection hardware. Combining dissimilar metals without considering the environmental conditions can introduce corrosion concerns. Outdoor and industrial installations deserve particular attention because moisture, chemicals, salt exposure, and temperature cycling can affect long-term performance.

For custom cable tray supports, fabrication may involve laser cutting, plasma cutting, forming, welding, machining, and finishing. These processes allow brackets, attachment plates, trapeze components, and support frames to be produced around project-specific geometry.

The important principle is that material selection and fabrication should support the engineering objective. A material should not be selected simply because it is commonly used elsewhere. Its structural performance, environmental resistance, connection compatibility, fabrication requirements, and project specifications should all be considered.

When Are Custom Cable Tray Supports and Strut Channels Needed?

Standard supports are effective for many installations, but unusual geometry, heavy loading, retrofit conditions, or limited structural attachment points can make custom cable tray support systems more practical.

A common example is a large cable tray that must pass through a congested mechanical room. Standard brackets may not provide the required clearance from ducts, pipes, structural members, or equipment. A custom support frame can be designed around those constraints while maintaining an appropriate structural connection.

High-density electrical systems can create another requirement. Multiple trays carrying substantial cable loads may require larger trapezes, reinforced frames, or custom attachment assemblies. The objective is not simply to create a stronger bracket; the support needs to fit the tray geometry, available structure, connection hardware, and installation sequence.

Retrofit projects can be particularly challenging. Existing buildings may have limited attachment locations, unexpected structural conditions, obsolete supports, or insufficient space for standard components. Custom brackets and attachment plates can provide a way to adapt the new cable tray system to existing conditions without unnecessarily modifying the building structure.

Custom strut channels can also address unusual support dimensions or interfaces. Fabricated steel assemblies may incorporate specific mounting holes, offsets, reinforcement, gussets, or connection plates required by the design.

The engineering-to-fabrication workflow is important:

Field Conditions → Engineering Requirements → 3D CAD → Fabrication Drawings → Cutting/Forming → Welding/Machining → Finishing → Inspection

The Sigma Source's combination of structural engineering, BIM 3D CAD, seismic calculations, and custom metal fabrication is particularly relevant when cable tray supports need to move from an engineering concept into a precisely fabricated assembly.

Custom fabrication should not be used simply to make a standard component look different. Its value comes from solving a defined engineering or installation problem—such as a difficult attachment, unusual geometry, large load, seismic restraint interface, or restricted installation envelope.

How Does BIM 3D CAD Improve Cable Tray Design and Installation?

BIM and 3D CAD can connect cable tray engineering with the actual spatial conditions of a building. Instead of evaluating the tray route independently, engineers and contractors can coordinate it with structure, HVAC, piping, electrical equipment, architectural elements, and other MEP systems.

Clash detection is one of the most obvious benefits. A support bracket may appear acceptable in two-dimensional plans but conflict with a structural beam or duct when viewed in three dimensions. Identifying that condition before fabrication reduces the likelihood of field modifications.

Three-dimensional coordination also helps with seismic bracing. Brace angles, attachment locations, structural members, and nearby systems can be reviewed together. This is especially useful where cable trays occupy congested mechanical or electrical rooms.

CAD models can also support fabrication. Once the support geometry is established, detailed fabrication drawings can communicate dimensions, plate thicknesses, hole locations, connection interfaces, weld requirements, and assembly information.

This creates a direct engineering-to-fabrication pathway:

Layout → Load Evaluation → Support Design → Seismic Analysis → BIM Coordination → Fabrication → Installation → Inspection

For contractors, the result can be clearer installation information. For engineers, it provides a better way to review spatial relationships and attachment conditions. For fabricators, it reduces ambiguity when producing custom support frames, brackets, strut components, and structural attachment assemblies.

BIM is not a substitute for engineering judgment. A visually coordinated model does not by itself establish load capacity, anchor capacity, seismic compliance, or structural adequacy. Those questions still require appropriate calculations, design criteria, manufacturer information, and professional review.

Its greatest value is integration. When cable tray routing, support geometry, structural attachment, and seismic restraint are developed in the same coordinated environment, the project team can identify conflicts earlier and maintain a clearer relationship between design intent and field installation.

What Codes and Standards Affect Cable Tray Systems and Seismic Support?

Cable tray projects in the United States can involve several layers of requirements. The applicable requirements depend on the project's jurisdiction, adopted code edition, building classification, system characteristics, specifications, and Engineer of Record criteria.

The International Building Code (IBC) provides a major framework for building design and can establish requirements affecting structural and nonstructural components. In California, the California Building Code (CBC) and locally adopted requirements become particularly important.

ASCE 7 provides seismic design provisions that can become relevant to nonstructural components and their supports. Chapter 13 is particularly important when evaluating applicable seismic requirements for building components and systems. The exact design process, however, should be based on the adopted standard and project-specific criteria rather than assuming that every cable tray installation receives the same treatment.

Healthcare projects can introduce additional requirements. Facilities under HCAI, formerly associated with OSHPD terminology, may have project-specific seismic, structural, documentation, and approval requirements. Cable tray support and restraint therefore need to be coordinated with the broader healthcare project.

Electrical installations may also involve the National Electrical Code (NEC), while NFPA requirements can apply depending on the building systems and project scope. UL-listed or approved components may be specified for particular applications.

Manufacturer installation instructions are another important design input. A listed or tested component should be installed according to its applicable requirements, and project specifications may impose additional criteria.

Compliance should therefore be treated as a project-specific engineering process:

Adopted Code → Project Criteria → Component Requirements → Seismic Demand → Support Design → Connection Design → Installation → Documentation

The Sigma Source's experience with seismic engineering, structural calculations, MEP restraint, BIM coordination, and HCAI/OSHPD-related applications provides a foundation for integrating these requirements into cable tray support projects without reducing compliance to a generic checklist.

How Are Cable Tray Systems Installed, Inspected, and Verified?

Installation quality determines whether the engineered cable tray system performs as intended in the field. Even a well-designed support assembly can be compromised if supports are relocated, anchors are installed incorrectly, braces are omitted, or field conditions differ from the design assumptions.

Installation begins with accurate tray routing and support locations. Trays should be aligned with the approved layout, while fittings and splice connections should be installed according to the applicable system requirements. Support assemblies need to maintain the intended geometry and attachment points.

Seismic brace installation requires additional attention. Brace orientation, connection locations, anchor installation, and attachment to the supporting structure should correspond with the engineered configuration. Unplanned relocation of a brace can alter its geometry and force path.

Field verification is especially important for renovation and retrofit work. Existing concrete thickness, reinforcement, structural steel locations, and available attachment points may differ from drawings. Where those differences affect the design, engineering review may be necessary before proceeding.

Inspection can examine tray alignment, support spacing, connections, anchors, fittings, brace configuration, clearances, and other project-specific requirements. Documentation may include fabrication drawings, engineering calculations, manufacturer data, installation information, inspection records, and approval documentation.

A useful verification sequence is:

Approved Design → Material Verification → Support Installation → Structural Attachment → Seismic Restraint → Tray Installation → Inspection → Documentation

This process creates traceability between the design and the installed system.

For large commercial, healthcare, industrial, and infrastructure projects, coordination among the electrical contractor, MEP team, structural engineer, general contractor, inspector, and fabricator can reduce field conflicts. The objective is not simply to install a cable tray that stays in place. The objective is to establish a support and routing system whose capacity, attachment, movement control, and installation correspond with the project's engineering requirements.

Conclusion: Engineering Cable Tray Systems as Complete Support Assemblies

Modern cable tray systems should be evaluated as complete engineered assemblies rather than as simple metal pathways. The tray carries the cables, but the performance of the installation depends on the interaction among tray geometry, cable loading, supports, connections, structural attachments, and—where required—seismic restraints.

A reliable design begins with the cable requirements and progresses through tray selection, width and depth, cable weight, support spacing, structural attachment, and coordination with other building systems. In seismic applications, the process continues through seismic demand, transverse and longitudinal restraint, connection capacity, anchorage, and the structural load path.

This integrated approach becomes especially important in high-density environments such as hospitals, data centers, industrial facilities, high-rise buildings, manufacturing plants, and critical infrastructure. These projects often combine substantial cable loads with limited space, complex MEP coordination, demanding structural interfaces, and detailed documentation requirements.

Material selection also needs to reflect the actual application. Carbon steel, structural steel, stainless steel, aluminum, galvanized components, protective coatings, and compatible hardware each have appropriate applications depending on structural, environmental, and fabrication requirements.

When standard components cannot address the installation, custom cable tray supports, support frames, attachment plates, and custom strut channels can be developed around the project's actual conditions. BIM 3D CAD can then connect the engineering model with fabrication and installation requirements.

The Sigma Source brings these disciplines together through seismic bracing, structural engineering, seismic calculations, BIM 3D CAD modeling, and custom metal fabrication. For cable tray projects, that integrated capability can support the progression from cable routing and loading through support design, structural attachment, seismic restraint, fabrication, and field installation—while keeping each decision tied to the specific requirements of the project.

Frequently Asked Questions About Cable Tray Systems

What are cable tray systems?

Cable tray systems are engineered pathways used to route and support electrical, communication, control, data, fiber-optic, instrumentation, and other cabling. A complete installation includes more than the tray itself. It can incorporate fittings, splice plates, brackets, hangers, trapeze supports, strut channels, structural attachments, and seismic restraint assemblies. The system needs to be evaluated as an interconnected assembly because cable weight is ultimately transferred through the tray and supports into the building structure.

How is cable tray support spacing determined?

Support spacing depends on tray configuration, material, width, depth, cable loading, span, allowable deflection, manufacturer information, support capacity, and project specifications. There is no universal spacing value suitable for every cable tray. Engineers should consider the tray, support members, connections, and structural attachments together rather than selecting spacing solely from a generic rule.

What is cable tray seismic bracing?

Cable tray seismic bracing is a restraint system designed to control earthquake-induced movement and transfer applicable seismic forces through the cable tray and its supporting structure. It differs from ordinary gravity support. A gravity support primarily carries normal vertical loads, while seismic restraint addresses movement and force transfer associated with earthquake design requirements.

Do cable tray systems require seismic bracing?

Whether seismic bracing is required depends on the applicable jurisdiction, adopted building code, seismic design criteria, component characteristics, project specifications, and Engineer of Record requirements. In projects where seismic restraint applies, the tray, support assembly, brace, connections, anchors, and supporting structure should be evaluated as one load path.

What is the difference between transverse and longitudinal cable tray bracing?

Transverse bracing generally controls movement perpendicular to the longitudinal direction of the tray. Longitudinal bracing addresses movement along the tray's primary direction. Depending on the system geometry and applicable design requirements, installations can use different restraint configurations, including arrangements intended to address movement in multiple directions.

Can strut channels support cable tray systems?

Yes. Strut channels can be used for trapeze supports, brackets, support frames, mounting rails, and seismic restraint assemblies. Their configuration depends on the tray loading, support span, structural interface, and project requirements. Custom strut channels may be useful where standard dimensions or configurations cannot accommodate the available space or attachment geometry.

How are cable tray supports attached to concrete?

Cable tray supports can be attached to concrete using appropriate anchorage systems, including mechanical or adhesive anchors where suitable for the specific application. The concrete substrate, anchor type, embedment, edge conditions, reinforcement, applied loads, and project requirements all need to be considered. Anchor selection should be based on the actual design rather than assuming that one anchor type is suitable for every condition.

How are cable tray supports attached to structural steel?

Steel attachments can use beam clamps, bolted brackets, welded assemblies, attachment plates, gusset plates, or other engineered connections. The connection must be compatible with the structural member and the loads being transferred. In seismic applications, the attachment also becomes part of the seismic force path and should be evaluated accordingly.

Are cable tray systems used in hospitals?

Yes. Hospitals and healthcare facilities use cable tray systems for power, communications, controls, data, fire alarm, and other electrical infrastructure. Healthcare projects can involve demanding coordination and seismic requirements. Projects under HCAI jurisdiction may also require specific documentation, approval, and restraint considerations.

When should custom cable tray supports be used?

Custom supports can be appropriate when standard components cannot efficiently accommodate unusual tray dimensions, heavy loading, limited structural attachment locations, retrofit conditions, congested MEP spaces, unusual offsets, or complex seismic restraint interfaces. Custom fabrication is most useful when it solves a defined engineering or installation constraint.

How does BIM improve cable tray engineering?

BIM and 3D CAD allow cable trays and their supports to be coordinated with structural framing, HVAC, piping, plumbing, electrical equipment, architecture, and other systems. This helps identify clashes before fabrication and installation. BIM can also support fabrication drawings by defining support dimensions, attachment locations, and assembly geometry.

What information is needed to design cable tray support systems?

Typical design inputs include tray type, width, depth, material, cable type and weight, expected fill, routing, span, support locations, structural attachment points, environmental conditions, and applicable seismic criteria. Structural and architectural drawings, BIM models, manufacturer data, and field measurements can also be important, particularly for retrofit projects.

Can The Sigma Source provide custom cable tray support solutions?

The Sigma Source combines seismic bracing, structural engineering, seismic calculations, BIM 3D CAD modeling, and custom metal fabrication. This capability can support cable tray applications requiring engineered trapeze assemblies, support frames, custom strut channels, structural attachment plates, seismic restraint assemblies, and other fabricated components based on project-specific conditions.

items.content_html:
Vibration isolation is rarely a matter of choosing a mount based on equipment weight alone. In demanding commercial, industrial, healthcare, marine, and infrastructure applications, the equipment, operating conditions, supporting structure, and required vibration performance must be considered as one connected engineering system. This is where custom isolator design becomes valuable.

A standard vibration mount may have an appropriate nominal load capacity but still be unsuitable because its stiffness, dimensions, mounting pattern, operating frequency range, environmental resistance, or movement characteristics do not match the application. A custom solution instead begins with the actual equipment requirements and develops the isolator around those conditions.

The engineering process can involve equipment weight and center of gravity, load distribution, operating speed, excitation frequency, static deflection, natural frequency, dynamic stiffness, damping, transmissibility, lateral loads, shock conditions, and available mounting space. Material selection also matters. Rubber compounds, spring steel, stainless steel, carbon steel, wire rope, and other materials behave differently under temperature, corrosion, fatigue, and cyclic loading.

Custom isolation may also need to interface with equipment bases, inertia bases, mounting frames, structural steel, concrete supports, flexible connections, and seismic restraints. For building applications, seismic requirements may introduce additional considerations under ASCE 7, IBC, CBC, or project-specific criteria, while healthcare facilities may have additional HCAI requirements.

For engineers, contractors, facility managers, and procurement teams, the objective is not simply to obtain a physically compatible mount. It is to develop an isolation system whose mechanical characteristics are appropriate for the equipment and whose physical configuration can be integrated into the project.

The Sigma Source approaches custom isolator design through this broader engineering perspective, connecting vibration isolation engineering with BIM 3D CAD modeling, structural analysis, seismic calculations, and precision fabrication when the application requires an integrated solution.

What Is Custom Isolator Design and When Is It Needed?

Custom isolator design is the engineering process of developing a vibration isolation component or assembly around the actual requirements of a particular piece of equipment. Rather than adapting the equipment to a catalog product, the isolation system is developed around the equipment's loading, excitation, geometry, environmental conditions, and performance objectives.

Standard vibration isolators remain appropriate for many applications. However, specialized equipment can create requirements that fall outside typical catalog configurations. An industrial machine may have an unusual bolt pattern or highly concentrated loads. A generator may produce significant dynamic forces while requiring both vibration isolation and seismic restraint. A marine engine may operate in a corrosive environment and experience continuous vibration and shock. An HVAC unit may have limited space beneath the equipment and require a custom mounting frame.

Custom Isolators vs. Standard Vibration Mounts

The difference is fundamentally an engineering issue rather than simply a dimensional one. A standard mount may have the correct nominal capacity but an unsuitable stiffness or deflection characteristic. Conversely, a mount with adequate stiffness may not fit the required footprint or provide the necessary movement control.

Custom design can address:

  • Unequal loads between mounting points

  • Unusual equipment footprints

  • Nonstandard bolt patterns

  • Low-frequency excitation

  • Variable operating speeds

  • High cyclic loading

  • Shock or transient loads

  • Restricted installation space

  • Corrosive or marine environments

  • Elevated temperatures

  • Special structural attachment requirements

Applications can include pumps, fans, compressors, chillers, air handling units, generators, motors, machine tools, production machinery, laboratory equipment, medical equipment, and marine engines.

The appropriate solution may be a custom spring isolator, wire rope isolator, rubber/metal mount, captive isolation assembly, or a more comprehensive equipment mounting system. In many projects, the isolator itself is only one part of the design. Custom brackets, mounting plates, rails, inertia bases, or structural frames may be required to establish a reliable interface between the equipment and the isolation system.

How Are Equipment Loads Determined for Custom Isolator Design?

The starting point for a custom vibration isolator is an accurate understanding of the equipment loads. Total equipment weight provides only the first level of information. Engineers also need to understand how that weight is distributed among the individual mounting points and how operating conditions modify the forces carried by each isolator.

Equipment Weight and Load Distribution

If a piece of equipment is supported by four isolators, it cannot automatically be assumed that each isolator carries exactly one-quarter of the total weight. The center of gravity, support geometry, equipment configuration, and stiffness distribution can produce different reactions at each mounting location.

This becomes especially important when equipment contains heavy motors, transformers, compressors, rotating assemblies, or other concentrated components. Load distribution should therefore be considered when determining the required capacity and stiffness of each individual mount.

Center of Gravity

The center of gravity influences both static loading and equipment stability. If the center of gravity is substantially above the support plane, lateral movement and overturning behavior can become more important. The position of the isolators relative to the equipment's center of gravity can affect rotational response as well.

Static and Dynamic Loads

Static load represents the equipment's supported weight. Dynamic loading can result from rotating imbalance, reciprocating mechanisms, torque reactions, startup and shutdown events, impact, or other operating conditions.

A custom isolator design therefore needs to distinguish between the equipment's static condition and its dynamic operating condition. Depending on the application, engineers may need to evaluate multiple load cases rather than designing around a single nominal weight.

Equipment Load Data

Useful inputs can include manufacturer data, equipment drawings, mounting dimensions, operating speeds, center-of-gravity information, vibration measurements, and known dynamic forces. When these inputs are incomplete, field measurements and additional engineering investigation may be necessary before finalizing the isolation system.

How Does Operating Frequency Affect Custom Vibration Isolator Design?

Operating frequency is one of the most important variables in vibration isolation. A mount that supports the equipment mechanically may still perform poorly as an isolator if its dynamic characteristics are inappropriate for the frequency generated by the equipment.

Equipment Operating Speed

Rotating machinery commonly produces excitation associated with operating speed. For example, an engine or motor operating at a specified RPM generates a corresponding fundamental rotational frequency, while imbalance and mechanical characteristics can introduce additional harmonics.

Reciprocating equipment can produce several excitation components, making frequency analysis more complex. Variable-speed machinery creates another challenge because the operating frequency may change during normal operation.

Natural Frequency

Every isolation system has a characteristic natural frequency influenced by supported mass and effective stiffness. For a simplified single-degree-of-freedom system, natural frequency is related to the ratio of stiffness to mass. This relationship is central to understanding whether an isolator can provide meaningful vibration isolation.

Isolation performance generally depends on the relationship between excitation frequency and the isolation system's natural frequency. When excitation occurs near resonance, vibration can become amplified rather than effectively isolated.

Resonance

A poorly selected isolator can place the system near a resonant condition during startup, shutdown, or normal operation. Custom isolator design can therefore consider the complete operating range rather than only the steady-state RPM.

Multiple Excitation Frequencies

Industrial machinery may have several excitation sources simultaneously. Engineers may evaluate the fundamental operating frequency, harmonics, gear-related frequencies, blade-pass frequencies, reciprocating forces, or other known sources.

This is one reason custom vibration isolation engineering should begin with the equipment's actual dynamic behavior. The objective is not simply to choose a softer or harder mount, but to establish a suitable relationship between equipment excitation and isolation-system response.

How Are Static Deflection, Stiffness, and Transmissibility Evaluated?

Static deflection, stiffness, damping, and transmissibility are closely connected in vibration isolation design. Treating any one of these parameters independently can produce an incomplete understanding of system behavior.

Static Deflection

Static deflection describes how much an isolator deflects under the supported equipment load. For spring isolation systems, static deflection is closely related to spring stiffness and supported mass and is an important design parameter when establishing the system's natural frequency.

Greater flexibility can support lower natural frequencies, but increased movement may also create clearance, stability, or restraint challenges. The appropriate deflection is therefore determined by the application rather than by a universal target.

Dynamic Stiffness

Dynamic stiffness describes how an isolator responds under dynamic loading. This can be particularly important for elastomeric materials, whose behavior may depend on frequency, temperature, preload, and material formulation.

The difference between static and dynamic properties means that a design based only on a static load rating may not adequately represent actual operating behavior.

Damping

Damping affects how energy is dissipated within the isolation system. It influences resonance amplitude, transient response, and the shape of the transmissibility response. Higher damping can reduce resonant amplification, although damping characteristics must be evaluated alongside isolation requirements.

Transmissibility

Transmissibility describes the relationship between the excitation and the vibration transmitted through the isolation system. It is affected by frequency ratio, damping, stiffness, and system configuration.

Consequently, claims such as a universal percentage of vibration reduction are rarely meaningful without specifying the frequency range, equipment, mount characteristics, loading, and installation conditions.

A technically sound custom vibration isolator design evaluates these variables together to establish an isolation system appropriate for the actual application.

What Types of Custom Vibration Isolators Can Be Designed?

Different equipment and operating environments call for different isolation technologies. Custom design allows the geometry and configuration to be adapted while preserving the fundamental behavior required by the application.

Custom Spring Isolators

Spring isolators can provide substantial vertical flexibility and are commonly considered for mechanical equipment such as HVAC units, pumps, fans, compressors, and other machinery. Depending on the application, configurations can include open, restrained, or captive springs.

The spring characteristics need to correspond to the supported load and desired dynamic response. Physical dimensions, mounting hardware, travel limits, and restraint requirements also influence the final design.

Custom Wire Rope Isolators

Wire rope isolators use formed wire rope elements to create a compliant support system. They can provide multidirectional flexibility and may be useful in applications involving vibration, shock, impact, or demanding environmental conditions.

Stainless steel wire rope configurations can also be considered where corrosion resistance is important, although material selection remains application-specific.

Custom Rubber and Elastomeric Isolators

Rubber and elastomeric systems can be designed using natural rubber, neoprene, synthetic rubber, laminated elastomers, or rubber/metal assemblies. Their properties can be tailored through material formulation and geometry.

These systems can be useful where compact dimensions, specific stiffness characteristics, or integrated mounting configurations are required.

Captive and Restrained Systems

Some equipment requires controlled movement in addition to vibration isolation. Captive or restrained isolation systems can incorporate mechanical features that limit excessive displacement while allowing the isolator to perform its intended vibration-control function.

The restraint must be designed as part of the complete system. Adding a rigid restraint without considering its interaction with the isolation system can unintentionally create a direct vibration path.

How Does Custom Isolator Design Address Mounting Geometry?

Mechanical compatibility is a fundamental part of successful vibration isolation. Even an appropriately engineered isolator is of limited value if it cannot be securely and accurately connected to the equipment and supporting structure.

Equipment Footprint and Mounting Points

Engineers may need to work around unusual equipment dimensions, existing bolt holes, limited underside clearance, or irregular support surfaces. The position of each isolator can affect load distribution, stability, and rotational behavior.

Custom mounting plates, brackets, rails, and attachment components can provide the necessary interface without requiring major modifications to the equipment.

Uneven Loading

Individual mounts may experience different loads because of equipment geometry or center-of-gravity location. Custom designs can accommodate these variations by assigning appropriate capacity or stiffness to different support locations.

Equipment Stability

A vibration isolation system must support the equipment while controlling unwanted movement. High or offset centers of gravity can increase the importance of lateral stiffness and rotational response.

The design may therefore consider vertical, horizontal, axial, lateral, and torsional behavior rather than treating the equipment as a simple vertically loaded mass.

Equipment Bases and Inertia Bases

In some applications, an inertia base or equipment mounting frame can help integrate the equipment with the isolation system. The fabricated assembly may incorporate steel plates, structural members, brackets, anchor points, and isolator attachment locations.

This approach is particularly useful when the equipment itself lacks suitable mounting geometry or when a larger support interface is required.

How Are Materials Selected for Custom Vibration Isolators?

Material selection is part of the engineering design because the material determines more than basic strength. Temperature, corrosion, fatigue, stiffness, environmental exposure, and service life can all influence material suitability.

Elastomer Selection

Natural rubber, neoprene, synthetic rubber, and other elastomeric compounds can have different mechanical and environmental characteristics. The appropriate compound depends on factors such as required stiffness, operating temperature, moisture, chemicals, ozone exposure, cyclic loading, and expected service life.

For this reason, a rubber isolator should not be specified solely by the generic term "rubber."

Spring and Metal Components

Spring steel is commonly associated with helical spring elements, while carbon steel, stainless steel, alloy steel, structural steel, and aluminum may be appropriate for housings, brackets, plates, frames, and other structural components depending on the application.

Stainless steel can be particularly relevant in corrosive or marine environments, but it should be selected based on the complete mechanical and environmental requirements.

Corrosion and Environmental Exposure

Industrial facilities, outdoor installations, wastewater environments, marine vessels, and coastal projects can expose components to moisture, salt, chemicals, and contaminants. Corrosion resistance should therefore be considered at the material, fastener, weld, and coating levels.

Protective Finishes

Galvanizing, powder coating, and other protective finishes can extend the service life of suitable components. However, coatings must be compatible with operating temperature and exposure conditions. A finish appropriate for a structural support may not be appropriate for a component exposed directly to elevated exhaust or engine temperatures.

How Does Custom Isolator Design Work With Seismic Restraint?

Vibration isolation and seismic restraint address different engineering problems, but they often need to coexist on the same equipment.

Vibration Isolation vs. Seismic Restraint

Vibration isolation is intended to reduce the transmission of operational vibration from equipment into its support structure. Seismic restraint is intended to control earthquake-induced movement and transfer applicable forces through the support and structural attachment system.

A vibration isolator should therefore not automatically be treated as a seismic restraint.

Isolated Mechanical Equipment

Equipment such as chillers, air handling units, pumps, generators, cooling towers, and other mechanical systems may require vibration isolation during normal operation while also requiring seismic protection based on the project's applicable criteria.

The challenge is maintaining the required isolation characteristics without creating an unintended rigid path around the isolator.

Captive and Restrained Configurations

Captive vibration isolators can incorporate movement-control features that limit displacement under specified conditions. The configuration must be engineered so that normal operating vibration isolation and required restraint behavior work together.

Structural Attachment

Seismic forces ultimately have to travel through a defined load path. Depending on the application, that path can involve the equipment, mounting frame, isolator or restraint assembly, attachment plate, anchor bolts or structural connection, and supporting concrete or steel structure.

Codes and Project Criteria

Where seismic protection applies, engineers may need to consider ASCE 7, the IBC, CBC, HCAI requirements, Seismic Design Category, Risk Category, nonstructural component provisions, and project-specific structural criteria.

Healthcare projects can require particularly careful coordination because equipment anchorage, MEP systems, support assemblies, and documentation may be subject to project-specific HCAI requirements.

The exact requirements depend on the adopted code edition, jurisdiction, equipment classification, project specifications, and Engineer of Record criteria.

How Does BIM 3D CAD Improve Custom Isolator Design?

Custom isolation often involves tight dimensional relationships between equipment, mounts, support structures, MEP systems, and architectural clearances. BIM and 3D CAD can make these relationships easier to evaluate before fabrication.

Equipment and Structural Coordination

A three-dimensional model can represent equipment dimensions, isolator locations, mounting plates, structural framing, piping, ductwork, electrical systems, and maintenance clearances in the same spatial environment.

This is particularly useful for mechanical rooms, rooftops, industrial facilities, data centers, and healthcare projects where available space can be highly constrained.

Clash Detection

Potential conflicts can include an isolator occupying the same space as a pipe, a mounting bolt interfering with structural steel, insufficient access for installation, or a seismic restraint conflicting with a flexible connection.

Identifying these issues before fabrication can reduce field modifications and coordination problems.

Design Documentation

CAD models can support dimensional drawings, fabrication details, mounting-hole patterns, assembly drawings, and equipment interface documentation. This information helps connect engineering analysis to manufacturing.

Engineering-to-Fabrication Workflow

A practical workflow can follow:

Equipment Data → Engineering Analysis → 3D CAD → Detailed Design → Prototype → Fabrication → Verification

This is particularly valuable when custom vibration mounts must be manufactured in low quantities or when an OEM requires repeatable mounting geometry.

The Sigma Source can combine BIM 3D CAD modeling with engineering and fabrication capabilities, allowing custom isolation assemblies to be developed with both performance and physical integration in mind.

When Are Custom Equipment Mounts, Bases, and Frames Required?

A custom isolator does not always need to be a standalone component. In many projects, the most effective engineering solution involves a complete mounting assembly that connects the equipment, isolators, and supporting structure.

Equipment Mounting Frames

A fabricated equipment frame can provide a common interface when the equipment footprint does not align with available isolator locations. Structural steel, sheet metal, plates, brackets, and custom attachment points can be integrated into the assembly.

Inertia Bases

An inertia base can form part of a broader vibration-control strategy for selected mechanical equipment. Its mass and stiffness characteristics, equipment attachment, isolator arrangement, and structural interface should be evaluated as a complete system.

Mounting Plates and Brackets

Custom plates can accommodate nonstandard bolt patterns, while brackets can address height differences, side mounting, or restricted access. CNC machining may be useful where tight dimensional tolerances or specialized interfaces are required.

Retrofit Applications

Existing installations can create additional constraints. Replacement equipment may not match the dimensions or anchor pattern of the original unit. Existing structural members may restrict where supports can be installed, while obsolete isolation hardware may no longer be available.

Custom fabrication can bridge these differences by producing new mounting plates, brackets, rails, frames, or isolation assemblies around verified field conditions.

Integrated Fabrication

Laser cutting, plasma cutting, forming, welding, machining, and other fabrication processes can support the transition from engineering drawings to finished assemblies. The goal is to maintain the specified geometry and interfaces rather than treating fabrication as a separate activity from design.

How Are Custom Isolators Fabricated and Verified?

Engineering performance and physical fabrication are closely connected. A theoretically appropriate isolator can still create problems if its dimensions, mounting interfaces, material specifications, or assembly geometry are not accurately produced.

Cutting and Forming

Laser and plasma cutting can produce plates, brackets, housings, and other custom components. Forming operations can create sheet-metal geometries that would be difficult or inefficient to manufacture from a standard product.

Welding and Machining

Welded steel assemblies can provide structural mounting interfaces, while CNC machining can support precision holes, plates, spacers, adapters, and specialized equipment connections.

Welding also requires attention to distortion, dimensional control, joint configuration, and the material being processed.

Prototype and First Article Fabrication

A prototype can be useful when the equipment interface is unusual or when a design has not previously been manufactured. A first-article component can also provide an opportunity to verify fit, mounting geometry, clearances, and assembly procedures before a larger production run.

Dimensional Verification

Verification can include checking mounting-hole locations, overall dimensions, plate thickness, attachment interfaces, isolator positioning, and assembly tolerances.

For equipment supplied to multiple facilities or an OEM program, repeatability becomes particularly important. The same isolation characteristics and physical interfaces need to be reproduced consistently across production units.

How Should Engineers Evaluate a Custom Isolator Design?

A custom isolator should be evaluated against the complete application rather than a single specification such as load capacity.

Performance Requirements

Important parameters can include:

  • Static deflection

  • Natural frequency

  • Dynamic stiffness

  • Damping

  • Transmissibility

  • Operating frequency

  • Expected vibration amplitude

  • Movement limits

  • Shock requirements

  • Transient response

These parameters should be evaluated together because improving one characteristic can influence another.

Mechanical Requirements

The evaluation should also consider equipment weight, load distribution, center of gravity, mounting geometry, attachment hardware, support spacing, structural interfaces, and applicable load cases.

Environmental Requirements

Temperature, moisture, chemicals, corrosion, marine exposure, contamination, and outdoor conditions can influence both materials and expected service life.

Durability

Continuous industrial operation can produce millions of loading cycles. Fatigue, material degradation, wear, and cyclic deformation therefore deserve consideration when designing isolation components for long-term service.

Verification

Depending on the application, verification may include engineering calculations, manufacturer material data, prototype evaluation, dimensional inspection, vibration measurements, or application-specific testing.

For seismic applications, structural calculations and anchorage evaluation may also be required. Compliance should be demonstrated against the actual project criteria rather than inferred simply because a component is marketed as a vibration isolator.

What Information Is Needed to Start a Custom Isolator Design?

Good input data can significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of the design process. The more clearly the equipment and installation conditions are defined, the less uncertainty exists between initial engineering and final fabrication.

Equipment Information

Useful information includes:

  • Equipment manufacturer and model

  • Operating weight

  • Overall dimensions

  • Center of gravity

  • Mounting points

  • Bolt-hole pattern

  • Equipment support surfaces

  • Operating speed

  • Manufacturer installation requirements

Dynamic Information

Where available, engineers should provide excitation frequencies, rotating or reciprocating characteristics, vibration measurements, startup and shutdown conditions, and known vibration problems.

If vibration data are unavailable, the equipment's operating characteristics can still provide an initial basis for analysis, followed by additional evaluation where required.

Structural Information

The design team may need information about the supporting slab, structural steel, equipment platform, existing anchors, available attachment points, and structural capacity.

For seismic applications, the project may also require seismic design criteria, component information, anchorage requirements, and EOR direction.

Environmental Information

Temperature, humidity, chemical exposure, marine conditions, outdoor installation, and corrosion risks can affect material and coating decisions.

Project Documentation

CAD files, BIM models, photographs, equipment drawings, existing isolation details, specifications, and field measurements can help establish the physical requirements.

The Sigma Source can connect this information across custom vibration isolation, vibration analysis, BIM 3D CAD modeling, structural engineering, seismic calculations, and custom metal fabrication, allowing the design to progress from equipment requirements to a manufacturable isolation assembly.

Conclusion

Effective custom isolator design begins with the understanding that vibration isolation is a system-level engineering problem. The isolator must support the equipment mechanically while providing dynamic characteristics appropriate for the equipment's excitation, operating frequency, loading, geometry, environment, and required vibration performance.

That process starts with accurate equipment data. Weight and load distribution establish the basic support requirements, while center of gravity and mounting geometry influence stability and individual isolator loading. Operating speed and excitation frequency then provide the dynamic context needed to evaluate natural frequency, stiffness, damping, and transmissibility. Material selection adds another layer, particularly when the equipment operates in marine, industrial, outdoor, high-temperature, or corrosive environments.

In many applications, the isolator cannot be considered independently from the equipment mounting system. Custom plates, brackets, inertia bases, equipment frames, structural supports, and flexible connections may all be required to establish the correct physical interface. When the equipment is installed in a seismically regulated building, vibration isolation may also need to coexist with seismic restraint and anchorage designed around applicable project criteria.

BIM and 3D CAD further connect engineering intent with physical implementation by allowing equipment, isolation components, structural supports, MEP systems, and clearances to be coordinated before fabrication. Prototype and first-article manufacturing can provide another level of validation for specialized applications.

The Sigma Source brings these disciplines together through engineering, vibration-control systems, seismic calculations, BIM/CAD modeling, and precision metal fabrication. This integrated approach is particularly relevant when standard products cannot accommodate the actual application and the isolation system must be developed around real equipment requirements.

The objective is not simply to produce a different-shaped mount. It is to develop an isolation solution whose load capacity, dynamic behavior, geometry, materials, structural interface, and installation requirements work together as an engineered system.

FAQ: Custom Isolator Design

What is custom isolator design?

Custom isolator design is the engineering process of developing a vibration isolation component or system around the requirements of specific equipment. It can account for equipment weight, load distribution, operating frequency, natural frequency, static deflection, dynamic stiffness, damping, mounting geometry, environmental exposure, and movement requirements.

Unlike selecting a standard mount solely from a load table, custom design considers how the isolator will behave within the complete equipment and support system.

When should a custom vibration isolator be used instead of a standard mount?

A custom solution may be appropriate when standard products cannot meet the required load, dimensions, stiffness, frequency response, mounting pattern, environmental resistance, movement limits, or structural interface.

This can occur with specialized industrial machinery, marine equipment, unusual HVAC installations, retrofit projects, OEM equipment, generators, machine tools, or applications with limited installation space.

What information is required for custom vibration isolator design?

Typical information includes equipment weight, dimensions, center of gravity, mounting points, operating speed, excitation frequencies, support arrangement, environmental conditions, and desired vibration performance.

Equipment drawings, manufacturer documentation, CAD models, photographs, existing isolation details, vibration measurements, and structural drawings can also help establish the design requirements.

What is the difference between spring, rubber, and wire rope isolators?

These isolation technologies have different mechanical characteristics. Spring isolators can provide significant vertical flexibility, while elastomeric isolators can be developed around specific stiffness and damping requirements. Wire rope isolators can provide multidirectional compliance and can be useful for applications involving vibration and shock.

The appropriate selection depends on equipment loading, excitation, movement, environmental exposure, fatigue requirements, and installation geometry. There is no single isolator type that is appropriate for every application.

Can custom isolators be designed for HVAC equipment?

Yes. Custom vibration isolation can be developed for air handling units, chillers, cooling towers, pumps, fans, compressors, boilers, generators, and other mechanical equipment.

The design may need to account for operating speed, equipment weight, support spacing, equipment base construction, flexible piping and duct connections, maintenance access, and seismic requirements where applicable.

Can a custom isolator also provide seismic restraint?

Vibration isolation and seismic restraint have different functions. The isolator is intended to reduce operational vibration transmission, while seismic restraint limits earthquake-induced movement and transfers applicable forces through the equipment support and structural attachment system.

Some applications can use captive or restrained isolation configurations, but the restraint must be engineered so it does not unintentionally create a rigid vibration path during normal equipment operation.

How does ASCE 7 affect custom isolator design?

ASCE 7 can become relevant when the isolation system is part of seismic protection for equipment or building systems. Depending on the project, engineers may need to consider seismic design category, component characteristics, seismic forces, anchorage, support conditions, and nonstructural component requirements.

The applicable provisions depend on the adopted code, project location, equipment classification, building characteristics, and project-specific engineering criteria. ASCE 7 should therefore not be treated as a universal design requirement for every vibration isolation application.

Are custom isolators used in healthcare facilities?

They can be used for healthcare HVAC systems, pumps, generators, mechanical equipment, laboratory equipment, and other applications where vibration control is important.

Healthcare projects may also involve additional seismic and documentation requirements. Where HCAI applies, equipment supports, anchorage, restraints, and related building-system components should be coordinated with the project's applicable HCAI requirements and Engineer of Record criteria.

Can custom isolators be fabricated for marine applications?

Yes. Marine equipment can create demanding requirements involving continuous vibration, shock, limited installation space, corrosion, moisture, and cyclic loading. Marine engine mounts and other custom isolation assemblies can therefore require careful material, geometry, stiffness, and fatigue considerations.

Stainless steel wire rope and corrosion-resistant metal components may be appropriate for selected marine environments, but material selection should be based on the actual exposure and mechanical requirements.

Does custom isolator design include custom mounting frames and brackets?

It can. A complete isolation system may require mounting plates, brackets, rails, equipment frames, inertia bases, structural supports, or custom steel assemblies.

These components can provide the interface between unusual equipment geometry and the selected isolators. They can also help coordinate equipment with existing structural steel, concrete supports, rooftop platforms, or retrofit conditions.

How does BIM 3D CAD support custom isolator design?

3D CAD and BIM can coordinate equipment dimensions, isolator locations, mounting interfaces, structural members, MEP systems, maintenance clearances, and seismic restraints.

This allows potential conflicts to be identified before fabrication and helps produce detailed manufacturing and installation information. For complex projects, the model can form an important connection between engineering analysis, fabrication, and field installation.

Can The Sigma Source support both engineering and fabrication?

The Sigma Source can connect custom vibration isolation with vibration-control engineering, BIM 3D CAD modeling, structural and seismic engineering, and custom metal fabrication.

Depending on project requirements, fabrication capabilities can include laser cutting, plasma cutting, forming, welding, machining, and production of custom steel assemblies, mounting components, and equipment support structures. This integrated approach is useful when the isolation solution requires both engineered performance and nonstandard physical components.
